lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Comparisons in writing
lessons.body: A simile compares things using like or as. Consider the effect of the comparison in its context, not just its label.

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Audience and purpose
lessons.body: Persuasive writing aims to influence a reader. Reasons relevant to the audience make a request more convincing.

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Evidence and inference
lessons.body: An inference is a supported conclusion, not a certainty. Check which detail supports your reading and avoid adding facts.

lessons.subject: gaeilge
lessons.title: Sonraí i dteachtaireacht
lessons.body: Léigh an teachtaireacht iomlán. Tabhair faoi deara focail a bhaineann le ham agus áit.

lessons.subject: gaeilge
lessons.title: Am i gcomhthéacs
lessons.body: Is féidir le focail ama cabhrú leat ord imeachtaí a thuiscint. Léigh an abairt agus lorg an leid ama.

lessons.subject: gaeilge
lessons.title: Lucht léitheoireachta agus réim
lessons.body: Braitheann an réim teanga ar an gcomhthéacs agus ar an lucht léitheoireachta. In iarratas foirmiúil, bí soiléir agus cúirtéiseach.

lessons.subject: history
lessons.title: Sources and historical questions
lessons.body: A primary source comes from the period or activity being studied. It can still be mistaken, selective or biased. Its usefulness depends on the question.

lessons.subject: history
lessons.title: Comparing evidence
lessons.body: Corroboration compares sources to test an account. Independent agreement can strengthen a claim but does not remove the need to evaluate context.

lessons.subject: history
lessons.title: Change and continuity
lessons.body: Change means something became different; continuity means something persisted across a period. Both can appear together.

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Poetry: the first read of an unseen poem
lessons.body: Read the poem twice before you answer. On the first read, work out who is speaking, who or what they are speaking to, and what is happening. On the second read, note repeated words, images, and any change of mood between the first and last lines. You should be able to say what the poem is about in one sentence before you write anything.

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Poetry: poetic devices and what they do
lessons.body: Name the device, then say what it makes the reader see or feel. A simile compares two things using like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another. Personification gives human qualities to something that is not human. Imagery uses the senses. Alliteration repeats starting sounds. Enjambment carries a sentence over a line break, so the reader keeps going. Example (original): My father comes home when the streetlights are already on, / his boots loud on the step like a clock that won't stop. The simile 'like a clock' makes the footsteps sound regular and unwelcome, as if time at home is being counted.

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Poetry: answering with Point, Quote, Explain
lessons.body: Point: answer the question in one clear sentence. Quote: choose a short phrase from the poem and copy it exactly. Explain: say what the word choice shows and why it matters to the poem's meaning. Use 'suggests' for an interpretation, because a poem can support more than one reading. In a short answer, write two or three paragraphs, each about a different device or idea. Check each paragraph: does it use the poem's own words, not only your opinion?

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Poetry: keep a short theme and image bank for studied poems
lessons.body: For each studied poem, write in your own words: the main theme, three images with the line each comes from, one device you noticed, and the feeling you think the poet wants the reader to have. Keep the bank short enough to revise in ten minutes. Use it to plan answers to theme prompts, which may ask about a studied poem in a new way. Your teacher's list decides which poems you study; ScoilMate does not reproduce published poems.

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Poetry: tone and the speaker's feeling
lessons.body: Tone is the attitude the poem takes, shown through word choice, rhythm and what is left unsaid. Tone words include weary, hopeful, angry, tender and lonely. Before you name a tone, test it: choose one word, then find two words or images from the poem that support it. If you cannot find evidence, choose another word. Speaker and poet are not always the same, so answer about the speaker's feeling when the question asks for it.

options.text: A shelter would keep students’ saddles dry during rain.

questions.explanation: It gives a benefit relevant to people who cycle to school.
hints: Think about what would persuade a school to provide a shelter.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Original micro-text: “Nora checked the clock twice and hurried towards the bus stop.” Which inference is best supported?

options.text: Nora may be worried about missing the bus.
Nora has already missed three buses.

questions.explanation: Clock-checking and hurrying support possible concern about time; the other claims lack evidence.
hints: Use only details in the sentence.
Checking time and hurrying can suggest urgency.

hints: Tá an cheist ag lorg áite.
Féach ar an bhfocal leabharlann.

hints: Smaoinigh ar cé a léifidh an t-iarratas.

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: A historian investigates a town market in 1910. Which is most directly a primary source for that investigation?

options.text: A market trader’s diary entry written in 1910.
A film review published last week.

questions.explanation: The contemporary diary is direct evidence from the period; it still needs evaluation and corroboration.
hints: Consider when each source was produced.
Which source was created during the period under investigation?
questions.provenance: Original ScoilMate draft; not copied or adapted from an examination paper.

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Two accounts give different dates for a local meeting. What is the best next step?

options.text: Look for independent contemporary evidence and compare origins.
Use the date in the newer book without checking.

questions.explanation: Independent evidence and source origins help assess conflicting accounts; length or publication recency alone does not settle it.
hints: Think about testing a claim rather than guessing.
Can another source help check the dates?

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: A town’s market moved indoors in 1950, but continued to open every Saturday. Which detail shows continuity?

options.text: The market still opened every Saturday.

questions.explanation: The Saturday schedule persisted even though the location changed.
hints: Look for what stayed the same.
Which detail describes an unchanged routine?

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: When you first read an unseen poem, what should you work out first?

options.text: The exact year the poem was written.
Who is speaking, to whom, and what is happening.
Whether you personally like the poem.

questions.explanation: The first read is about the basic situation. It gives you what you need to say what the poem is about.
hints: Start with the basics: the speaker, the listener and the situation.
Which choice helps you say what the poem is about?

his boots loud on the step like a clock that won't stop.

questions.explanation: 'Like a clock' compares the boots to a clock using 'like', so it is a simile.
hints: Look for a comparison that uses the word like or as.
Which line compares the boots to something else?

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: In the example, the first line ends with 'already on,' and the sentence carries on into the next line. What is this called?

options.text: Enjambment: the sentence runs over the line break.
A spelling choice by the poet.

questions.explanation: Enjambment means the sentence continues past the end of a line, so the reader keeps moving forward.
hints: Look at whether the sentence finishes at the end of the line.
Which choice describes a sentence that continues onto the next line?

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: An original poem says: 'The canal holds its breath all winter.' Which device is 'holds its breath'?
questions.explanation: A canal cannot breathe, so the poet gives it a human action. That is personification.
hints: Is a human action being given to something that is not human?
Which device gives human qualities to a thing?

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt:
Read this original poem:
Nobody sits on the bench since the advert went up, / the glass is cracked and the timetable has faded to blue. / Still I wait here, counting the buses that do not come, / the way you count the stairs in a house you have left.
Which word best describes the tone?
questions.explanation: 'Faded', 'do not come' and 'left' show tiredness and a sense of waiting without reward.
hints: Look at words such as 'faded', 'cracked' and 'do not come'.
Which word fits a speaker who is tired of waiting?

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt:
Read this original poem:
The river keeps its coat of ice until March, / then gives it back in small bright plates on the brown water.
What does 'coat of ice' most suggest?

options.text: The ice is dirty and unwanted.
The river is covered as if wrapped up for winter.
The river is warm in summer.
The ice is part of a school uniform.

questions.explanation: The metaphor of a coat suggests the river is wrapped and protected by ice through winter.
hints: A coat keeps something warm and covered. What is the river wrapped in?
Which choice explains the image rather than repeating the words?

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt:
Read this original poem:
You never left the light on for me, / yet I walk home each night towards the window / that is always dark.
Which word best describes the speaker's feeling?
questions.explanation: The light is never on and the speaker keeps going back to a dark window, which suggests loneliness.
hints: Focus on the image of the dark window.
Find one line that shows the speaker is left waiting.
